fixes.explanation: I see the thinking, but there's no city gate in this verse. Leviticus 14:3 says, “The priest is to go outside the camp to examine him…” The person had been living outside the camp (Leviticus 13:46), so that's where the priest goes. A gate would've been a shorter walk, friend, but the verse sends him past the camp.

The altar is a good guess, since offerings come later in this chapter. But for this bird, Leviticus 14:7 says the priest releases it into the open field. The other bird is the one slaughtered. This one gets let go.

Nope, the priest's tent isn't in this verse. It says the person “…must remain outside his tent for seven days.” His tent, not the priest's. He's back in the camp, and his own tent is the one that matters here.

The Tent of Meeting does show up in this chapter, but not here. Leviticus 14:8 says he “…must remain outside his tent for seven days.” That's his own tent, in the camp he's now allowed to enter. The Tent of Meeting comes into play on the eighth day (Leviticus 14:11).

At the entrance to the Tent of Meeting is right. Leviticus 14:11 says the priest presents the person with the offerings “…before the LORD at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.” That's the spot for the eighth day. The person stands there with his offerings, and the priest who performs the cleansing presents him.

The open field is where the live bird was released (Leviticus 14:7). Here, the person and his offerings are presented “…at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.” Different moment, different spot. Easy to mix up with all this walking around.

By this point, the healing has already happened. The priest began the cleansing after he examined the person and found “…the skin disease of the afflicted person has healed…” (Leviticus 14:3). The oil on his head is “…to make atonement for him before the LORD.” (Leviticus 14:18). So the text gives atonement as the purpose, not healing.

The text doesn't say the priest chooses. Leviticus 14:22 says, “…two turtledoves or two young pigeons, whichever he can afford…” The measure is what the person can afford. The priest's part comes after, when he sacrifices the birds, one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering (Leviticus 14:30-31).

Cleared is right. Leviticus 14:36 says, “The priest must order that the house be cleared before he enters it to examine the mildew…” So the order comes before he goes in. The text gives the reason too: “…so that nothing in the house will become unclean.”

It's false, friend. If the mildew comes back and spreads after the replastering, the text calls it “…a destructive mildew; the house is unclean.” (Leviticus 14:44). Then comes verse 45: “It must be torn down with its stones, its timbers, and all its plaster…” The text sends the house to be torn down, not scraped again.
